title: Magik Yup’ik
bodyHtml:
Central Alaskan Yup'ik belongs to the Eskimo-Aleut language family. It is spoken in western and southwestern Alaska by around 20,000 speakers. Two other Yup'ik languages are still spoken: the Alutiiq language and the Siberian Yup'ik language.

Yup'ik people have an interesting concept when it comes to counting — the words for the numbers can be broken down into meaningful parts which may be related to their body parts. For example, the word for five, talliman, means an arm and the word for six, arvinlegen, means cross over, as you need to change hand to go on counting.

The Yup'ik people often include geometry in their Yup'ik parkas, often having border patterns. One such pattern comes in the form of a 3 by 3 square (the rows and columns are numbered 1–3; the three cells of the top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal are shaded in the booklet):

1 2 93
2
3

A magic square can be constructed by placing the digits 1 to 9 within the cells such that the sum of all the digits in every row, column, and diagonal is the same.

To help you fill in the magic square, the following clues are given in Yup'ik. The numbers are spelled (i.e. 123 is spelled as “One hundred and twenty-three” in English). HINT: The Yup'ik name for the number 294 is yuinaat qula cetaman qula cetaman.

AcrossDown
1Yuinaat yuinaq cetaman qula malruk1Yuinaat yuinaq atauciq akimiaq pingayun
2Yuinaat akimiaq malruk akimiaq malruk2Yuinaat yuinaak malruk yuinaat malrunglegen qula atauciq
3Yuinaat yuinaak malruk akimiaq atauciq3Yuinaat qula pingayun akimiaq atauciq

Answer these questions in the Answer Sheets.

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the numbers missing from the magic square above.

questions.promptHtml: Write the Yup'ik spelling of the three-digit number read down the shaded diagonal.
questions.partPrompt: In Yup'ik, write the number given in 1-Diagonal (Top left cell to Bottom right cell, shaded).

hints.text: Start with the arithmetic, not the language. There is really only one 3-by-3 magic square using the digits 1 to 9 (the other seven versions are just rotations and mirror images of it), and the centre cell is forced. The 9 that is already printed in the top middle tells you which rotation you are looking at.

Every clue is a three-digit number and every clue begins with the same word, so Yup'ik cannot be counting in tens. Yup'ik counting is built on fingers plus toes, so try base 20. Then look at the word endings: -k marks a dual (multiply by two), -t marks a plural, and a word ending in -q is a bare root, telling you the next number is added rather than multiplied.

Practise on the number the problem gives you for free: 294 is yuinaat qula cetaman qula cetaman. In base 20, 294 = (20 x 14) + 14. So yuinaat means "twenties of" (multiply by 20) and qula cetaman must be 14, i.e. qula = 10 plus cetaman = 4. Now use the same method on a clue such as 2-Across, which reads akimiaq malruk twice.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: solve the magic square as pure arithmetic

A 3-by-3 magic square holds the digits 1 to 9 with every row, column and diagonal adding to the same total. Call the centre number n. Every one of the 9 digits appears once, and 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45. The three columns each add to the same amount, so that amount is 45 / 3 = 15. Working from the centre, the whole square can be written as

n-1n+4n-3
n-2nn+2
n+3n-4n+1

Each row, column and diagonal here adds to 3n, and since the grand total is 9n = 45, we get n = 5. That gives the classic square. There are eight ways to write it down (four rotations, each of which can also be mirrored), but the 9 already printed in the top middle picks out exactly one of them — and the Yup'ik clues confirm it.

Step 2: notice that Yup'ik is not counting in tens

Down clue 2 fills the middle column, whose top digit is the given 9, so that clue names a number in the 900s. Yet the clue is only six words long and starts with the same word as every other clue, yuinaat. Since Yup'ik counting is based on fingers and toes, the natural guess is base 20 (a vigesimal system: the counting unit is 20 rather than 10).

Step 3: decode the free example

The problem tells us 294 is yuinaat qula cetaman qula cetaman. In base 20, 294 = (20 x 14) + 14. The clue is yuinaat followed by the same two words twice, so:

  • yuinaat = "twenties of", i.e. multiply what follows by 20;
  • qula cetaman = 14, which must be qula = 10 added to cetaman = 4.

The endings carry the arithmetic: -k is a dual ending (times two), -t is plural (times more than two), and a word ending in -q is the plain root, signalling that the next number is added instead of multiplied.

Step 4: check the clues against the square

Down clue 2, Yuinaat yuinaak malruk yuinaat malrunglegen qula atauciq, parses as (20 x 20 x 2) + (20 x 7) + (10 + 1) = 800 + 140 + 11 = 951 — and the middle column of the square does read 9, then 5, then 1. Similarly Across clue 3, Yuinaat yuinaak malruk akimiaq atauciq, is (20 x 20 x 2) + 16 = 816, matching the bottom row, and it tells us akimiaq atauciq = 16. Since atauciq = 1 (from 951), akimiaq = 15 — a sensible word for a Yup'ik counter, since 15 is "both hands and one foot".

Down clue 3, Yuinaat qula pingayun akimiaq atauciq, is (20 x (10 + 3)) + 16 = 276, the right-hand column. Piecing the vocabulary together: atauciq = 1, malruk = 2, pingayun = 3, cetaman = 4, qula = 10, akimiaq = 15, yuinaq = 20.

Step 5: write the shaded diagonal in Yup'ik

Read the shaded diagonal from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell to get a three-digit number. Now spell it in base 20. It splits as (20 x something) + 16, and 16 is akimiaq atauciq. The multiplier is more than 20, and the other clues show that numbers in this range are not built with a second yuinaak: instead the multiplier itself is spelled as 20 plus a remainder, using the root form yuinaq to signal addition. So the answer is Yuinaat + (20 + 2) + 16.

Point split is inferred: 1 point per magic-square cell (8) plus 7 for G2, since the solution shows no per-part breakdown. In the booklet the grid is a shaded checkerboard (corners and centre shaded), which highlights the top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal referred to in G2; the HTML table cannot show shading, so this is stated in prose instead. Cell labels (a)-(h) and the small row/column numbers 1-3 are printed in the booklet grid and are reproduced as blank labels / superscripts.
